note: Cards for the substantive lessons written in the second pass. Section numbers are the point of most of these, and every one carries the source it came from.

cardTypes.term: Defined term or Latin maxim. Irreducible pair.
cardTypes.rule: A black-letter rule or a single element of one.
cardTypes.ratio: The principle a case stands for.
cardTypes.source: Where a rule comes from — statute, section, or authority.
cardTypes.trigger: A fact cue that should make you think of a doctrine.

cards.front: Which Article makes federal law prevail over inconsistent State law?
cards.back: Article 75. The State law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.

cards.front: What are the three lists in the Ninth Schedule?
cards.back: List I Federal, List II State, List III Concurrent — with supplementary lists for Sabah and Sarawak.

cards.front: Land is a State matter. How can the National Land Code be a federal statute?
cards.back: Article 76 lets Parliament legislate on State matters for uniformity; the law takes effect in a State on adoption by its legislature.

cards.front: What does Article 4(1) provide?
cards.back: The Constitution is the supreme law; law inconsistent with it is void to the extent of the inconsistency.

cards.front: A federal statute is passed on a List II subject. What is the first question?
cards.back: Competence, not Article 75. An ultra vires federal law prevails over nothing.

cards.front: What did the 1988 amendment do to Article 121(1)?
cards.back: It replaced the vesting of judicial power in the courts with jurisdiction 'conferred by or under federal law'.

cards.front: What does Article 121(1A) do?
cards.back: It removes from the civil courts jurisdiction over matters within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts.
cards.note: It is a subtraction from the civil courts, not a grant to the Syariah courts.

cards.front: What is the basic structure doctrine?
cards.back: The argument that certain fundamental features cannot be removed even by a valid constitutional amendment.
cards.source: Malaysian and Indian constitutional case law

cards.front: Which court decides whether a law is invalid for want of legislative competence?
cards.back: The Federal Court, exclusively, under Article 128.

cards.front: Where does the burden of proving a general exception lie, and to what standard?
cards.back: On the accused, on the balance of probabilities — s 105 of the Evidence Act 1950.

cards.front: Which section makes every Penal Code offence subject to the general exceptions?
cards.back: Section 6 of the Penal Code.

cards.front: Section 79 of the Penal Code excuses a mistake of what?
cards.back: A mistake of fact, made in good faith. Mistake of law does not excuse.

cards.front: When is there no right of private defence under s 99(3)?
cards.back: Where there is no reasonable apprehension of death or grievous hurt and there is time to have recourse to the public authorities.

cards.front: An accused kills while exceeding the right of private defence. What should you reach for?
cards.back: Exception 2 to s 300 — murder may be reduced to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

cards.front: What does 'non-bailable offence' mean?
cards.back: Bail is in the court's discretion, subject to s 388 — not that bail is unavailable.

cards.front: Where is an offence classified as bailable or non-bailable?
cards.back: The First Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code, offence by offence.

cards.front: How long may a person be held after arrest without a Magistrate's authority?
cards.back: Twenty-four hours — Article 5(4) of the Federal Constitution. Longer needs a remand order under s 117 CPC.
cards.source: Federal Constitution Art 5(4); Criminal Procedure Code s 117

cards.front: What is the question at the close of the prosecution case?
cards.back: Whether a prima facie case has been made out — s 180 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

cards.front: What is a discharge not amounting to an acquittal?
cards.back: A discharge that leaves the accused liable to be recharged on the same facts.

cards.front: Which section lists what makes consent not free?
cards.back: Section 14 of the Contracts Act 1950: coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation, mistake.

cards.front: What is the effect of coercion, fraud or misrepresentation on an agreement?
cards.back: It is voidable at the option of the party whose consent was so caused — s 19(1).

cards.front: What is the effect of a bilateral mistake as to an essential fact?
cards.back: The agreement is void — s 21. There is nothing to affirm.

cards.front: When is silence fraud under s 17?
cards.back: Where there is a duty to speak, or where silence is in itself equivalent to speech.

cards.front: Which section requires restoration of an advantage received under a void agreement?
cards.back: Section 66 of the Contracts Act 1950.

cards.front: Which section measures damages for breach of contract in Malaysia?
cards.back: Section 74 of the Contracts Act 1950 — the rule in Hadley v Baxendale, enacted.
cards.source: Contracts Act 1950, s 74; Hadley v Baxendale (1854) 9 Exch 341

cards.front: Which section governs a sum named in the contract as payable on breach?
cards.back: Section 75 of the Contracts Act 1950 — reasonable compensation, not exceeding the sum named.

cards.front: What did Cubic Electronics v Mars Telecommunications decide about s 75?
cards.back: It reformulated the Malaysian approach, moving away from the strict proof-of-actual-loss requirement in Selva Kumar and asking whether the clause protects a legitimate interest.
cards.source: Cubic Electronics Sdn Bhd v Mars Telecommunications Sdn Bhd [2019] 6 MLJ 15 (FC)
cards.note: Verify this citation and check for anything decided since.

cards.front: Which statute governs specific performance in Malaysia?
cards.back: The Specific Relief Act 1950 — not the Contracts Act.

cards.front: What does s 40 give a promisee faced with an entire refusal to perform?
cards.back: The right to put an end to the contract, unless he has acquiesced in its continuance.

cards.front: State the but-for test.
cards.back: But for the defendant's breach, would the damage have occurred? If it would, causation fails.

cards.front: Which provision governs contributory negligence in Malaysia?
cards.back: Section 12 of the Civil Law Act 1956 — apportionment, not a complete defence.

cards.front: State the remoteness rule.
cards.back: The kind of damage must be reasonably foreseeable; the extent need not be.

cards.front: Novus actus interveniens versus contributory negligence — what is the difference?
cards.back: The first breaks the chain and defeats the claim; the second reduces the damages.

cards.front: What are the three elements of defamation?
cards.back: The words are defamatory, they refer to the plaintiff, and they were published to a third party.

cards.front: What is publication in defamation?
cards.back: Communication to at least one person other than the plaintiff.

cards.front: Where does malice bite in a defamation action?
cards.back: It defeats qualified privilege and fair comment. It is not an element of the tort.

cards.front: What does s 8 of the Defamation Act 1957 do?
cards.back: Justification does not fail merely because every charge is not proved true, if the rest do not materially injure reputation.

cards.front: When does a dealing pass an interest in registered land?
cards.back: On registration. Before that the purchaser has contractual and equitable rights only.

cards.front: Who may enter a private caveat?
cards.back: A person claiming title, or any registrable interest, or to be beneficially entitled under a trust affecting the land — s 323.

cards.front: What must a caveator show on an application to remove a private caveat?
cards.back: A serious question to be tried, and that the balance of convenience favours maintaining the caveat.
cards.source: Malaysian case law on private caveats

cards.front: Where does a chargee apply for an order for sale?
cards.back: Registry title: the High Court. Land Office title: the Land Administrator.
cards.source: National Land Code, the order-for-sale provisions

cards.front: What did Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San decide?
cards.back: It restored deferred indefeasibility under s 340, departing from Adorna Properties.
cards.source: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC)

cards.front: Which provision states a director's duty to act in good faith in the company's best interest?
cards.back: Section 213(1) of the Companies Act 2016. Section 213(2) is the duty of care.

cards.front: What does a statutory derivative action require?
cards.back: Leave of the court, good faith, and that the action is prima facie in the company's best interest.

cards.front: Which section gives the oppression remedy?
cards.back: Section 346 of the Companies Act 2016.

cards.front: What is reflective loss?
cards.back: A fall in share value caused by harm to the company. The claim belongs to the company, not the member.

cards.front: Which section places the legal burden on the person who would fail if no evidence were given?
cards.back: Section 102 of the Evidence Act 1950.

cards.front: What is the scope of s 106?
cards.back: A specific fact especially within a person's knowledge. It cannot reverse the general burden.

cards.front: 'May presume', 'shall presume', 'conclusive proof' — what is the difference?
cards.back: A discretion; mandatory unless disproved; and admitting no evidence in rebuttal.

cards.front: What is illustration (g) to s 114?
cards.back: That evidence which could be and is not produced would, if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it.

cards.front: What must be established before any question of burden arises?
cards.back: Admissibility. Relevance is defined by the Act, not at large.

cards.front: What must a defendant show to resist summary judgment under Order 14?
cards.back: A triable issue, or some other reason why there ought to be a trial — not that the defence will succeed.

cards.front: On a strike-out for no reasonable cause of action, what evidence is admissible?
cards.back: None. The question is taken on the pleading as it stands.

cards.front: State the interlocutory injunction test.
cards.back: A serious question to be tried; damages an inadequate remedy; balance of convenience — with an undertaking in damages.
cards.source: Rules of Court 2012, O 29; American Cyanamid as applied in Malaysia

cards.front: What is the general limitation period for contract and tort?
cards.back: Six years from the accrual of the cause of action, under the Limitation Act 1953.

cards.front: Audi alteram partem — what does it require?
cards.back: Notice of the case against you and a fair opportunity to answer it.

cards.front: What is the practical test for bias?
cards.back: Whether a fair-minded and informed observer would conclude there was a real danger, or real possibility, of bias.
cards.source: Malaysian and English case law on bias
cards.note: Check which formulation the Malaysian courts currently use.

cards.front: Can a legitimate expectation arise from a representation outside the decision-maker's power?
cards.back: No. A public body cannot bind itself to act unlawfully.

cards.front: What are the three classic grounds of judicial review?
cards.back: Illegality, irrationality, procedural impropriety — with proportionality argued as a fourth.
cards.source: The GCHQ classification as received in Malaysia

cards.front: What are the two procedural thresholds under Order 53?
cards.back: Leave of the court, and an applicant who is adversely affected by the decision — within the prescribed time.
